title: The body: elements
hookLine: like a butcher who has divided a carcass: earth, water, fire, air (MN 10)
last: THE BODY — A BAG OF GRAIN.

cards: Put your hand flat on a table. Feel the hardness under your palm. Now the warmth of your own hand, and maybe a slight dampness.
Then the tiny movements: the pulse, the breath shifting your shoulders. Hard, wet, warm, moving.
Those four make an old way of sorting what a body is made of, and the Satipatthana Sutta uses them to look at the body from one more angle.

teach.b: The practitioner reviews this very body, however it is placed, however it is disposed, by way of the elements. In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element.
Each is a dhatu, an element, and in Buddhist teaching they're less like substances, more like qualities you can feel. Earth is hardness and solidity: bones, teeth, the weight in your seat.
Water is cohesion and fluidity: blood, sweat, the way things hold together. Fire is heat: warmth, digestion, the burn of a fever. Air is movement: the breath, the pulse, the push and pull inside.
Then the image, and it's a blunt one.
A skilled butcher, or his apprentice, has killed a cow and divided it at a crossroads, and sits with it cut into portions.
The commentaries explain the point: before, he thought of it as a cow; now he sees only portions of meat. The name has fallen away, and what's left is just what's there.

teach.h: THE BODY IS MADE OF THE WORLD.
teach.b: Looking at the body by elements does the same to the word me.
Instead of a single, solid self, you find hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that are in the table, the rain, the sun and the wind. It isn't meant to be cold.
Some practitioners describe it as a relief: the body is made of the world, and belongs to it.

how: Meditators in several Buddhist traditions practice elements meditation by feeling hardness, cohesion, heat and motion in the body; in some Burmese and Thai lineages it is a core practice for seeing the body as not-self.

o: earth, water, fire and air: hard, fluid, warm, moving
the four chemical substances that make up matter
four moods of a person, from calm to fiery

games.q: match each element to what you feel.

s: the four elements here are chemical substances
in Buddhist teaching they're qualities you can feel: hard, fluid, warm, moving.
the butcher simile is about how a name falls away
the cow becomes portions; the body becomes elements, not a solid me.
the same four elements are found outside the body too
earth, water, fire and air in the table, the rain, the sun and the wind.

games.q: a butcher sits at a crossroads with a divided carcass. what has changed in how people see it?
o: nothing: it's still called a cow.
the name 'cow' has fallen away; now it's portions of meat.
games.why: the simile shows a name dropping away. looking at the body by elements loosens the idea of a solid me the same way.

practice: Feel earth, the solid seat and the weight of your hands; water, the moisture in your mouth and the way the body holds together; fire, the warmth of your hands or a cool spot on your skin; air, the breath moving and the pulse if you can find it.
Then rest in all four at once, solid, fluid, warm, moving, and let the word me soften a little.

wordCard.voice: The body, elements. Earth, water, fire and air: hardness, fluid, warmth and motion, the same four that make up the world.

orig.note: Pali dhātu: an element, like earth, water, fire or air.

carryVoice: Your line: four elements. Even a sip from a cup holds all four. Two hundred fifty-four days now.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga XI (definition of the four elements)
